chunks: "The short version is that an NFET is the better transistor and a PFET is the easier one to drive.
For the same die area, an NFET has roughly two to three times lower on-resistance, because electrons are more mobile than holes.
So for a given R DS(on) the NFET is smaller, which means less gate charge and less output capacitance, so lower switching loss and lower cost.
That's why high-current or high-frequency converters use NFETs. The catch is the high side.
An NFET's source is the switch node, which swings up to V in , so to turn it on you need the gate about 5 volts above V in .
That takes a bootstrap capacitor and diode or a charge pump, and it limits the maximum duty cycle, because the bootstrap cap needs the low side to turn on periodically to recharge.
A PFET's source sits at V in . You turn it on by pulling the gate down toward ground and off by pulling it up to V in , so no bootstrap.
It can also stay on forever, so 100% duty and low dropout. The cost is area, gate charge and capacitance, so more loss at high frequency.
I'd use a PFET for low input voltages and simplicity, and an NFET when efficiency or current matters."
